Fossilized hatchlings of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis indicate that neonates emerged from the egg measuring roughly 12 centimeters [Lb = roughly 12 centimeters] in total length, a dimension that implies a relatively altricial state at hatching. This modest size at birth, derived from the dimensions of the pelvic canal in adult specimens, suggests that the initial growth phase was rapid, as juveniles needed to quickly attain a body size capable of evading the small theropod predators common to the Early Cretaceous ecosystems of Central Asia. The hatchling length is consistent with the small egg volume inferred for this taxon, which likely produced clutches of multiple relatively small eggs. Neonatal body proportions appear to have been broadly similar to those of adults, with a relatively large head and hindlimbs already adapted for bipedal or facultatively bipedal locomotion. This early morphology underscores the precocial nature of the hatchlings, which were probably capable of limited mobility shortly after emergence. The total length at birth represents a foundational point for modeling growth trajectories, as subsequent increases in body size reflect the species' overall life-history strategy of moderate to rapid somatic development before the onset of reproductive activities.

As individuals matured, Psittacosaurus mongoliensis attained a formidable ultimate total length of approximately 200 centimeters [Li = approximately 200 centimeters], a value reconstructed from the largest known nearly complete skeletons within the species. This maximum size, placing the species among the larger members of its genus, was likely reached after several years of sustained growth. The pronounced size increase from the roughly 12 centimeter hatchling length to the ultimate length reflects a growth pattern characterized by sustained, though not necessarily rapid, osseous accretion over the juvenile and sub-adult periods. The ultimate length is also consistent with the species' proposed ecological role as a medium-sized, low-browsing herbivore, a niche that benefits from a body size large enough to deter predators but not so large as to require exceptionally high food intake. The attainment of this final size is tightly linked to sexual maturation, as adult skeletal features, including fusion of vertebral elements, are rarely observed in specimens below this length. This maximum body dimension thus marks the culmination of the species' somatic growth phase and the transition to full reproductive status.

Analyzing growth curves derived from femoral cross-sectional histology and a body mass regression for ornithischian dinosaurs, researchers estimated that the ultimate wet weight of Psittacosaurus mongoliensis was in the range of 25,000 grams [Wwi = in the range of 25,000 grams]. This projection provides a valuable anchor for understanding the species' energetic requirements and trophic impact within its paleocommunity. A mature individual of this mass, roughly comparable to a modern medium-sized peccary, would have required a daily intake of fibrous plant material substantial enough to sustain its basal metabolic processes and activity. The estimated adult mass also allows paleobiologists to infer fundamental life-history parameters, such as the species' relative metabolic rate and its reproductive investment per offspring. While the confidence interval around this estimate is somewhat broad due to the inherent uncertainties in extrapolating soft tissue from skeletal dimensions, it nevertheless offers one of the more robust mass estimates for any non-ceratopsid neoceratopsian. This mass value is critical for comparisons with other basal ceratopsians that occupied similar ecological niches in the Early Cretaceous.

Working under the assumption that the metabolic and reproductive physiology of basal neoceratopsians operated at typical endothermic avian or high-performance reptilian body temperatures, and given the consistent thermal regime of the Early Cretaceous Jehol Biota, experimental life-history models have been calibrated at a reference temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At this thermal baseline, estimates of lifespan for Psittacosaurus mongoliensis have been calculated from growth-ring counts and asymptotic size, leading to a proposed maximum longevity of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This lifespan, while speculative, aligns with the documented growth patterns in long-bone histology, which show a gradual decline in the rate of circumferential expansion after the first few years. The attainment of a 30-year lifespan indicates a moderately slow life-history pace relative to small theropods from the same deposits, but a faster one compared to derived, larger ceratopsids. This longevity has direct implications for population dynamics and generation time, suggesting that adult mortality rates from predation must have been relatively low to sustain such extended individual survival. The 37 °C thermal context is crucial, as metabolic rates and senescence processes are inherently temperature-sensitive in all amniotes.

Further life-history analyses conducted at the same reference body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] suggest that Psittacosaurus mongoliensis reached sexual maturity, marked by the onset of reproductive capability, at around 10 years after hatching [tp = around 10 years after hatching]. This relatively late maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy favoring sustained somatic growth before diverting resources to reproduction. The extended juvenile period likely allowed individuals to attain a body size sufficient to navigate the competitive and predatory landscape of their environment before investing in egg production. By integrating this age at maturity with the estimated 30-year maximum lifespan, the species appears to have had a reproductive window of approximately two decades, ample time to produce multiple clutches. This pubertal timing correlates with the attainment of approximately 60 to 70 percent of the ultimate body mass, a threshold commonly observed in extant reptiles and birds. The maximum rate of reproduction, though highly speculative, has been modeled from clutch size and the duration of the nesting season to yield approximately ten offspring per year per female [Ri = approximately ten offspring per year per female], assuming an optimal thermal and resource environment at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This annual reproductive output would have been sufficient to offset juvenile mortality and maintain stable population sizes in the dynamic lake-margin environments of the Jehol Group.
